title: Navratri Begins: Celebrating Nine Nights of Devotion and Joy
excerpt: Join the vibrant festivities of Navratri, honoring the divine feminine.
body:
• Sharad Navratri 2026 runs October 11–19, culminating in Dussehra on October 20 and leading into Diwali on November 8.
  • Each of the nine nights honors a different form of Goddess Durga, with a traditional color assigned to every day.
  • Celebrations span Garba and Dandiya dances, Durga Puja pandals, fasting, and nightly prayers — with diaspora communities gathering in temples and community centers across the US.

Navratri — literally "nine nights" — begins today, October 11, 2026. It is the most important festival dedicated to Goddess Durga, marking the victory of good over evil and the celebration of divine feminine energy. The nine nights honor the Navadurga, the nine forms of the goddess, each worshipped on a successive day: Shailaputri, Brahmacharini, Chandraghanta, Kushmanda, Skandamata, Katyayani, Kalaratri, Mahagauri, and Siddhidatri.

This year's Sharad (autumn) Navratri runs from Sunday, October 11 to Monday, October 19. Because of a tithi overlap, Durga Ashtami and Maha Navami both fall on October 19 this year. The festival concludes with Vijayadashami — Dussehra — on Tuesday, October 20, which in turn opens the road to Diwali, falling on Sunday, November 8, with Dhanteras on Friday, November 6.

Each day of Navratri carries a traditional color, and devotees — especially in Maharashtra and Gujarat — dress accordingly. This year's sequence: orange (Oct 11), white (Oct 12), red (Oct 13), royal blue (Oct 14), yellow (Oct 15), green (Oct 16), grey (Oct 17), purple (Oct 18), and peacock green (Oct 19).

How It's Celebrated

Celebrations vary dramatically by region. In Gujarat and among Gujarati communities worldwide, the nights belong to Garba and Dandiya Raas — energetic folk dances performed in large circles to live music and drums, often continuing past midnight. In West Bengal, Assam, and Tripura, the same nine nights are Durga Puja: elaborately decorated pandals housing towering idols of the goddess, with cultural programs, dhunuchi dances, and community feasts.

In Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, the festival takes the form of Golu — tiered displays of dolls and figurines in homes, with neighbors visiting each other's displays. In North India, many devotees observe fasts, some abstaining from grains entirely and eating only fruits, milk, and specific fasting foods like sabudana (tapioca) and kuttu (buckwheat) preparations. Nightly aartis and kirtans complete the devotional rhythm.

The Diaspora Angle

For Indian-American families, Navratri is one of the most community-driven festivals of the year. Temples and cultural organizations across the US organize Garba nights that draw thousands — the events listed below are just a sample of what's happening today. Many families use the nine nights to teach children the stories behind each form of Durga, turning the festival into a living lesson in heritage.

Practical note for US celebrations: most community Garba events sell out, especially weekend nights. Book tickets in advance, arrive early for parking, and check whether your local temple requires registration for the nightly aartis during the week.
